title: Control Theory and PID

mentor.name: LAMBDA
mentor.character: Teaches by making the machine misbehave first, then asking you which term caused it.

summary: You will build a PID controller from the error signal up, with anti windup, filtering, feedforward and cascades, and tune it with both hand methods and Ziegler-Nichols. By the end you can stabilise an inverted pendulum in code and say when a PID is the wrong tool.

lessons.title: The Spire Wakes
lessons.goal: Write an open loop command and state why it cannot correct itself.
lessons.theory:
An **open loop** controller sends a command and never checks what happened. You tell a Pololu 25D gearmotor driver to run at 60 percent duty and you hope the wheel turns at the speed you wanted. Nothing in the code ever asks the wheel.

This works while the world stays exactly as it was when you calibrated. The moment the battery drops from 12.4 V to 11.1 V, or the robot climbs a ramp, the same 60 percent duty produces a different speed. The controller does not know and cannot care.

Open loop is not a mistake. It is the right answer for a stepper driving a 3D printer axis, or for a heating element that only has to be roughly warm. It becomes a mistake the moment the load changes and precision matters.

In this course every loop is a Python function that takes a measurement and returns a command. Today the function ignores the measurement on purpose, so you feel what is missing.
lessons.task: Write `open_loop(setpoint_rpm)` that converts a target speed into a motor duty cycle between 0.0 and 1.0 using the calibration constant `DUTY_PER_RPM`. Clamp the result to that range.
lessons.hint: The calibration says 200 rpm at full duty, so duty is the target divided by 200.

lessons.title: The Eye on the Shaft
lessons.goal: Read a measurement into the loop and compare it against the command.
lessons.theory:
A loop becomes **closed** the moment a sensor value enters the decision. On a wheel that sensor is usually a quadrature encoder on the motor shaft, a 12 count per revolution disc behind a 34:1 gearbox. On an oven it is a thermocouple. On a balancing robot it is an MPU-6050.

The measurement is never the truth. It is the truth plus noise, plus a delay, plus whatever the sensor does not see. A good controller treats it as evidence, not as gospel.

The first thing you do with a measurement is compare it to what you asked for. Not react, not correct, just compare. Everything in control theory grows out of that comparison.
lessons.task: Write `report(setpoint, measured)` that returns the string `"target 100.0 actual 92.0 gap 8.0"` using one decimal for each number, and print it for three sample readings.
lessons.hint: The gap is the setpoint minus the measurement, and `%.1f` gives you one decimal.

lessons.title: The Distance Between Want and Have
lessons.goal: Compute the error signal and keep its sign meaningful.
lessons.theory:
The **error** is `e = setpoint - measurement`. That order is not arbitrary. Written this way a positive error means you are below target and need to push harder, which matches the intuition of every actuator command you will ever write.

If you flip it to `measurement - setpoint` the whole controller inverts. It still works, as long as every gain is negative, but the first person to read the code will misjudge a sign and drive the robot into a wall. Pick the standard order and never change it.

Error has units. If the setpoint is in rpm, the error is in rpm. If it is in degrees, the error is in degrees. Every gain you write later is a conversion from those units into actuator units, which is why gains are not portable between machines.
lessons.task: Write `error(setpoint, measured)` and use it plus `report` from the previous lesson to print a line for each of four encoder readings.
lessons.hint: One line of body: subtract the measurement from the setpoint.

lessons.title: Which Way Is Up
lessons.goal: Choose a sign convention for the actuator and detect an inverted loop.
lessons.theory:
A loop with the wrong sign does not misbehave slightly. It runs away. Positive error asks for more push, the push moves the plant further from the target, the error grows, and the command saturates in under a second.

The sign depends on wiring, not on theory. Swap the two motor leads on a TB6612FNG driver and a perfectly tuned controller becomes a machine that slams into the end stop. The same happens if you mount the encoder on the other side of the gearbox.

The cheap test: give a small constant command, watch the measurement. If the measurement moves toward the setpoint, the sign is right. If it moves away, negate the command or fix the wiring. Do this before you tune anything.
lessons.task: Write `loop_sign_ok(before, after, command)` that returns True when a positive command increased the measurement and a negative command decreased it, and False otherwise.

    return True

print(loop_sign_ok(0.0, -12.0, 0.2))
print(loop_sign_ok(50.0, 44.0, -0.2))

lessons.title: The Loop That Never Sleeps
lessons.goal: Build the read, compute, write, wait skeleton every controller in this course uses.
lessons.theory:
Every controller in a real robot is the same four steps repeated forever: **read** the sensor, **compute** the command, **write** it to the actuator, **wait** until the next tick. On a Raspberry Pi 4 running a Python loop, that tick is typically 5 to 20 ms.

The wait is not politeness. It is the definition of your sample time, and every gain you tune assumes it stays constant. A loop that runs as fast as it can is a loop whose behaviour changes when you add a print statement.

In this course the plant lives in a function so the loop is testable without hardware. A first order plant like a motor with inertia moves toward its command with a time constant, and `plant_step` below is exactly that model.

lessons.title: The First Push
lessons.goal: Implement proportional control and see the command shrink as the error shrinks.
lessons.theory:
**Proportional control** is one line: `u = Kp * e`. The further you are from the target, the harder you push. As you arrive, the push fades to nothing.

That fade is the whole point. A bang bang controller pushes at full power until it crosses the target and then slams the other way. A proportional controller eases off, which is why a P loop on a wheel sounds smooth and a thermostat clicks.

`Kp` has units. If the error is in rpm and the command is a duty cycle from 0 to 1, then `Kp` is duty per rpm, and a value like 0.004 is normal. A `Kp` of 1.0 in that system would mean full power at one rpm of error.
lessons.task: Write `p_control(setpoint, measured, kp)` returning the proportional command, and run the plant for 60 steps with `kp = 0.004`, printing the final speed.
lessons.hint: The body is the error from the last chapter multiplied by kp.

lessons.title: Turning the Knob
lessons.goal: Compare rise time across several values of Kp on the same plant.
lessons.theory:
Raising `Kp` makes the loop react harder to the same error, so the response gets faster. On a 25D gearmotor you hear it: a soft gain makes the wheel creep up to speed, a stiff gain snaps it there.

There is no free speed. Every increase in `Kp` costs you stability margin, and past a certain point the loop overshoots, then rings, then oscillates without ever settling. The useful range usually spans one order of magnitude, not five.

The honest way to compare gains is not to look at a plot and guess. Measure. Rise time is the number of samples until the measurement first reaches 90 percent of the speed the loop actually settles at. Not 90 percent of the setpoint: a pure P loop stops short of the setpoint, and at these gains it stops short by so much that a threshold set on the setpoint would never be crossed and every gain would report the same nothing.
lessons.task: Write `rise_steps(kp, setpoint, limit)` that runs the loop, reads the settled speed off the end of the trace, and returns how many steps it took to first reach 90 percent of that speed. Print it for three gains.
lessons.hint: The settled speed is the last sample of the trace. Walk the trace from the start and return the index of the first sample at or above 90 percent of it.

lessons.title: The Gap That Will Not Close
lessons.goal: Explain and measure the steady state error left by a pure P controller.
lessons.theory:
Run a P loop long enough and it stops moving while still short of the target. This leftover is **steady state error**, and it is not a bug.

The logic is airtight: the motor needs some duty to hold 100 rpm against friction. That duty can only come from `Kp * e`. If `e` were zero the command would be zero and the wheel would stop. So the loop settles exactly at the error that produces the duty it needs.

Raising `Kp` shrinks the gap but never removes it, because the required duty is fixed by physics. The classic industrial name for this is **droop**, and it is the reason the integral term exists.
lessons.task: Write `steady_error(kp)` that runs 600 steps with a setpoint of 100 and returns the remaining error. Print it for three gains and confirm it shrinks but stays above zero.
lessons.hint: Run the loop to the end, then return the error one last time.

lessons.title: Why the Spire Shakes
lessons.goal: Show that a plant with delay swings harder as Kp rises, right up to the gain where it stops settling.
lessons.theory:
The first order plant you have been using never truly oscillates, no matter how high `Kp` goes. Real hardware does, because real hardware has **delay**.

A command written to a motor driver does not reach the shaft instantly, and an encoder reading arrives from a period you already left. When the controller reacts to old news, its correction lands after the plant already moved, so the correction is now in the wrong direction. Push hard enough on stale information and the loop swings.

That is the mechanism behind every ringing PID you will ever meet: gain multiplied by delay. Reduce either one and the ringing dies.

Pick the gains so the loop actually crosses the setpoint before you measure how far past it went. A pure P loop settles short of the setpoint, and below `kp` around 0.026 this one never reaches 100 at all, so an overshoot measured against the setpoint would read zero for every small gain and tell you nothing about damping. Above the gains printed below the swing keeps growing until it stops coming back: this loop still settles at `kp` 0.060 and no longer settles at 0.062.

    speed = 0.0
    pipe = [0.0] * DELAY
    peak = 0.0

lessons.title: The Load Fights Back
lessons.goal: Measure how a P loop responds to a sudden load disturbance.
lessons.theory:
A disturbance is anything that moves the plant without going through your command: a robot rolling onto carpet, a gripper picking up a 500 g payload, a fan blowing across a heated block.

A P loop rejects disturbances the same way it tracks setpoints. The load pulls the speed down, the error grows, the command grows, and a new equilibrium appears with more duty and a slightly worse steady state error than before.

How much the speed sagged and how fast it came back are the two numbers that matter in the field. Setpoint tracking looks good in a demo; disturbance rejection is what keeps a robot straight on a ramp.

lessons.title: Bias, the Cheap Fix
lessons.goal: Add a feedforward bias to a P loop and cut the steady state error without extra gain.
lessons.theory:
If the droop comes from the duty the motor needs at the operating point, you can just hand it that duty. `u = u0 + Kp * e`, where `u0` is a constant chosen for the expected load.

This is the smallest possible **feedforward**, and it is worth knowing before the integral term because it explains what the integral is really doing: finding `u0` on its own, slowly, by trial.

The weakness of a fixed bias is obvious. Change the load, change the battery, change the temperature, and `u0` is wrong again. It buys accuracy at the price of assuming the world holds still.

lessons.title: The Slowest Honest Loop
lessons.goal: Estimate the time constant of a plant from its own step response.
lessons.theory:
A first order plant answers a step command with an exponential rise. After one **time constant** it has covered 63.2 percent of the distance, after three it is within 5 percent, after five it is done for any practical purpose.

You can measure this on real hardware in one minute: command a fixed duty, log the encoder speed, find the time at 63.2 percent of the final value. That number, plus the final value, is a model good enough to tune a PID.

Doing this before tuning saves hours. A plant with a 0.35 s time constant and a 5 ms loop is easy. A plant with a 40 s time constant, like a heated bed, needs completely different gains and a much slower loop.
lessons.task: Write `time_constant(duty)` that runs the plant open loop, finds the step where speed first passes 63.2 percent of its final value, and returns that step multiplied by `DT`.
lessons.starter:
TAU = 0.35
DT = 0.02
GAIN = 180.0

def time_constant(duty, steps=400):
    speed = 0.0
    trace = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        speed = speed + (GAIN * duty - speed) * (DT / TAU)
        trace.append(speed)
    # TODO: find when the response has covered most of its distance, and return that time
    return 0.0

print(round(time_constant(0.5), 3))
lessons.solution:
TAU = 0.35
DT = 0.02
GAIN = 180.0

def time_constant(duty, steps=400):
    speed = 0.0
    trace = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        speed = speed + (GAIN * duty - speed) * (DT / TAU)
        trace.append(speed)
    target = 0.632 * trace[-1]
    for i, v in enumerate(trace):
        if v >= target:
            return (i + 1) * DT
    return steps * DT

print(round(time_constant(0.5), 3))
lessons.hint: The final value is the last element of the trace, and 0.632 of it is the threshold.

lessons.title: Reading the Shape of an Answer
lessons.goal: Compute overshoot, rise time and settling time from a response trace.
lessons.theory:
Three numbers describe a step response well enough to argue about it. **Overshoot** is how far past the setpoint the peak went, as a percentage. **Rise time** is how long it took to first reach the setpoint. **Settling time** is when it stopped leaving a 2 percent band around the setpoint.

They trade against each other. Every tuning decision you make in the next chapters buys one and sells another, and knowing which one your machine cares about is more useful than any tuning table.

A gantry that must not crash wants zero overshoot and accepts slow. A drone attitude loop wants speed and tolerates a few percent of overshoot. Same math, opposite tunes.

        trace.append(speed)

lessons.solution:
TAU = 0.35
DT = 0.02
GAIN = 180.0
DELAY = 2
BIAS = 0.55

def response(kp, setpoint=100.0, steps=500):
    speed = 0.0
    pipe = [0.0] * DELAY
    trace = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        pipe.append(BIAS + kp * (setpoint - speed))
        speed = speed + (GAIN * pipe.pop(0) - speed) * (DT / TAU)
        trace.append(speed)
    return trace

def metrics(trace, setpoint, dt):
    peak = max(trace)
    overshoot = max(0.0, (peak - setpoint) / setpoint * 100.0)
    rise = len(trace) * dt
    for i, v in enumerate(trace):
        if v >= setpoint:
            rise = (i + 1) * dt
            break
    band = 0.02 * setpoint
    settle = 0.0
    for i in range(len(trace) - 1, -1, -1):
        if abs(trace[i] - setpoint) > band:
            settle = (i + 1) * dt
            break
    return {"overshoot": round(overshoot, 2), "rise": round(rise, 3), "settle": round(settle, 3)}

print(metrics(response(0.02), 100.0, DT))
lessons.hint: Walk the trace backwards to find the last sample outside the 2 percent band.

lessons.title: The Controller Becomes an Object
lessons.goal: Wrap proportional control in a reusable class with a reset method.
lessons.theory:
From here on the controller carries state, so it stops being a function and becomes an object. A class gives you three things a function cannot: gains that live with the instance, memory between calls, and a `reset` you can call when the robot is disabled.

That `reset` matters more than it looks. A balancing robot that is picked up, moved and put down again must not resume with the state it had while dangling in the air. Every real controller has a way to be cleared.

The interface stays the same for the rest of the course: build it with gains, call `update(setpoint, measured, dt)`, get a command.

TAU = 0.35
DT = 0.02

class PController:
    def __init__(self, kp):
        self.kp = kp
        self.last_error = 0.0

    def update(self, setpoint, measured, dt):

        return self.kp * error

    def reset(self):
        self.last_error = 0.0

speed = 0.0
for _ in range(300):
    speed = speed + (GAIN * c.update(100.0, speed, DT) - speed) * (DT / TAU)

lessons.hint: `update` saves the error into `self.last_error` before returning the command.

lessons.title: What the Loop Remembers
lessons.goal: Accumulate the error over time and understand what the sum represents.
lessons.theory:
The **integral term** adds up every error the loop has ever seen, multiplied by the time it lasted: `I = I + e * dt`. It is a running memory of how long you have been wrong and by how much.

Why that helps is the key insight. Proportional control cannot produce output at zero error. Integral control can, because the accumulator keeps its value even when the error reaches zero. It is the term that finds the `u0` you hardcoded in the last chapter.

The accumulator has units of error times seconds. On a speed loop that is rpm seconds, which is a distance. That is not a coincidence: an integral of speed is position.
lessons.task: Write `accumulate(errors, dt)` that returns the running integral as a list, and print the last value for a list of constant errors.
lessons.starter:
DT = 0.02

def accumulate(errors, dt):
    total = 0.0
    out = []
    # TODO: carry a running total of how long you have been wrong
    return out

for errors in ([5.0] * 100, [5.0, -5.0] * 50):
    out = accumulate(errors, DT)
    print(len(out), [round(v, 3) for v in out[-1:]])
lessons.solution:
DT = 0.02

def accumulate(errors, dt):
    total = 0.0
    out = []
    for e in errors:
        total = total + e * dt
        out.append(total)
    return out

for errors in ([5.0] * 100, [5.0, -5.0] * 50):
    out = accumulate(errors, DT)
    print(len(out), [round(v, 3) for v in out[-1:]])
lessons.hint: The total grows by `e * dt` each sample, and errors of opposite sign cancel.

lessons.title: Ki and the Meaning of Time
lessons.goal: Apply the integral gain and reason about its units.
lessons.theory:
The integral contribution to the command is `Ki * I`. Because `I` carries a factor of seconds, `Ki` has units of command per error per second. A `Ki` of 0.01 on a duty and rpm system means a constant error of 1 rpm adds 0.01 duty every second.

That framing tells you how to pick a first value. Ask how long you are willing to wait for the loop to close a persistent 10 rpm gap. If the answer is two seconds and the missing duty is about 0.05, then `Ki` is roughly 0.05 divided by 10 divided by 2, which is 0.0025.

Engineers who prefer the standard form write `Ti = Kp / Ki`, the integral time, in seconds. Same controller, friendlier number: `Ti` is how long the integral takes to repeat the proportional action.
lessons.task: Write `pi_command(setpoint, measured, kp, ki, integral, dt)` returning both the command and the updated integral as a tuple.
lessons.starter:
DT = 0.02

def pi_command(setpoint, measured, kp, ki, integral, dt):
    error = setpoint - measured
    # TODO: update the integral and return (command, integral)
    return 0.0, integral

integral = 0.0

    print(round(u, 5), round(integral, 4))
lessons.solution:

def pi_command(setpoint, measured, kp, ki, integral, dt):
    error = setpoint - measured
    integral = integral + error * dt
    command = kp * error + ki * integral
    return command, integral

integral = 0.0
for _ in range(5):
    u, integral = pi_command(100.0, 90.0, 0.004, 0.01, integral, DT)
    print(round(u, 5), round(integral, 4))
lessons.hint: Update the integral first, then use it in the command you return.

lessons.title: Killing the Droop
lessons.goal: Prove that a PI loop drives the steady state error to zero.
lessons.theory:
Give the loop an integral term and the droop disappears. Not shrinks: disappears. As long as any error remains, the accumulator keeps growing, the command keeps rising, and the only place the system can rest is exactly at the setpoint.

This is worth stating precisely because it is the single strongest argument for the I term. A P loop settles where the error produces the needed command. A PI loop settles where the error is zero and the accumulator produces the needed command.

On a motor this is the difference between a wheel that runs at 96 rpm when you asked for 100 and one that runs at 100 flat, on carpet and on tile.

        speed = speed + (GAIN * duty - speed) * (DT / TAU)
        speed = speed - LOAD * DT
    return setpoint - speed

lessons.title: The Slow Swing

The integral is a lagging term. It reacts to the past, so its correction always arrives late. Push `Ki` too high and the accumulator overshoots the amount of command actually needed, the plant sails past the setpoint, and the accumulator has to unwind before the loop can come back.

The resulting oscillation has a distinct signature: slow, wide, and roughly symmetric, quite unlike the fast buzzing of an excessive `Kp`. Learning to tell those two apart by shape is half of manual tuning.

This is also why you never fix a sluggish loop by adding integral. Sluggishness is a proportional problem; the integral only fixes offset.

lessons.title: The Accumulator That Would Not Stop
lessons.goal: Reproduce integral windup by driving the loop against a saturated actuator.
lessons.theory:
Ask a motor for 400 rpm when it can only do 180. The error never closes, so the accumulator grows every single sample, forever. The command is already at 1.0 duty and the extra accumulation does nothing except pile up.

Then you lower the setpoint to something reachable. The error flips sign, but the accumulator holds an enormous positive value, so the command stays pinned at full power while the integral slowly unwinds. The wheel screams past the new target for seconds.

This is **windup**, and it is the single most common bug in hand written PID code. Any controller whose actuator can saturate, which is every controller on a real robot, needs protection against it.

lessons.title: The Diagnosis

You cannot fix windup you cannot see. The detector is simple: keep both the raw command and the clamped command, and flag the sample whenever they differ.

That flag is worth logging on real hardware, and the number it produces is meant to land between the extremes. A driver that never clips tells you nothing and a driver that clips on every sample tells you only that the setpoint is impossible. The interesting reading is the one in between: a robot whose driver spends 30 percent of its time saturated is not badly tuned, it is undersized, and no amount of gain adjustment will fix a motor that cannot deliver the torque.

This plant tops out at 180 rpm, so 100 rpm is comfortable, 177 rpm is the margin where the answer stops being yes or no, and 400 rpm is never coming.

The same flag becomes the trigger for the anti windup schemes in the next lessons, so build it now as a returned value rather than a print.

lessons.title: Clamping the Memory
lessons.goal: Bound the integral so it cannot grow past what the actuator can use.
lessons.theory:
The crudest working fix is an **integral clamp**. Decide the maximum contribution the integral is allowed to make, usually the full actuator range, and limit the accumulator to that.

The clamp is expressed in accumulator units, so it is `limit / Ki`. Writing it that way means the clamp stays correct when you retune `Ki`, which a hardcoded number does not.

It is not the most elegant scheme, and it can still hold the loop pinned longer than needed, but it is three lines and it turns a robot that overshoots for four seconds into one that overshoots for a quarter of one.

Measure it on a setpoint the motor can actually hold. Ask for more speed than the machine can deliver and the peak you print is just the top speed of the motor, the same number with the clamp and without it, and the comparison tells you nothing.

def run(setpoints, kp=0.004, ki=0.05, clamp=False):

lessons.title: Bumpless
lessons.goal: Handle setpoint changes and controller re-enable without a jump in the command.
lessons.theory:
Two moments break naive PID code. The first is a large setpoint step, where the accumulated history belongs to a target that no longer exists. The second is switching from manual to automatic, where the integral is stale or zero and the command jumps.

The fix for re-enable is to **preload** the integral with whatever command the actuator is already producing, so the first automatic sample outputs exactly what the manual mode did. The transfer is then invisible.

On a robot this is what lets you take over a wheel by hand, release it, and have the loop resume without a lurch. Any controller that can be disarmed needs this, and an autonomous robot is disarmed every time it hits an e-stop.

        self.integral = 0.0

Everything from this chapter belongs in one class: gains, accumulator, output limits, a clamp sized from those limits, and a reset that preloads.

Keep the interface honest: `update` takes `dt` as an argument rather than assuming a constant, because chapter 5 will make you regret any controller that assumes its own timing.

lessons.title: The Slope of the Error
lessons.goal: Compute the derivative of the error from consecutive samples.
lessons.theory:
The **derivative term** looks at how fast the error is changing: `D = (e - e_prev) / dt`. It is the only part of a PID that knows about the future, and it knows it the cheap way, by assuming the current trend continues.

If the error is shrinking fast, the derivative is large and negative, and `Kd * D` subtracts from the command. The controller eases off before arriving. That is braking.

The divide by `dt` matters. Skip it and your `Kd` silently changes meaning every time you change the loop rate, which is exactly the bug that makes a controller that worked on a desktop fail on a Raspberry Pi under load.

lessons.title: Braking Before the Wall
lessons.goal: Use Kd to cut the overshoot of a PI loop on a delayed plant.
lessons.theory:
A PI loop on a plant with delay overshoots because both of its terms react to error that already exists. The derivative reacts to error that is about to stop existing, so it pulls the command down while the plant is still approaching.

How much it buys depends on how much of the overshoot is dead time and how much is accumulated integral. On the plant below, a quarter of a second of transport delay against a 0.35 second time constant, the peak falls from 35 percent over the setpoint to 11 percent. Nothing else changed, the loop simply stops pushing earlier.

There is a limit, and it is close. Past `kd` around 0.001 the peak climbs again, and past 0.0018 the loop stops settling at all and rings forever. Tune `Kd` up from zero, watch overshoot fall, and stop at the bottom of the curve rather than beyond it.

lessons.title: The Noise Amplifier
lessons.goal: Show that the derivative term multiplies sensor noise by 1 over dt.
lessons.theory:
An encoder gives you counts, and a count either arrived or it did not. At a 5 ms loop that quantisation looks like noise of a few rpm bouncing around the true value. The proportional term sees a few rpm. The derivative sees a few rpm divided by 0.005, which is hundreds.

Multiply that by `Kd` and the command becomes a buzz. The motor heats, the driver whines, and the loop is technically stable while sounding broken. On an MPU-6050 the same effect turns gyro noise into visible twitching.

The rule to remember: the derivative gain amplifies high frequency content by a factor proportional to frequency. Any noise your sensor has, the D term will find.

lessons.title: A Filter for the Slope
lessons.goal: Apply a first order low pass filter to the derivative and pick its cutoff.
lessons.theory:
Nobody ships a raw derivative. The standard fix is a first order low pass on the D term: `d_filtered = d_filtered + alpha * (d_raw - d_filtered)`, where `alpha = dt / (tau_f + dt)`.

Choosing `tau_f` is a trade. Too small and the noise survives. Too large and the derivative lags so much that it stops predicting and starts fighting. A common starting point is `tau_f = Kd / (N * Kp)` with N between 8 and 20, which is the derivative filter every industrial PID block exposes.

The honest way to say it: the D term is only useful over a band of frequencies. The filter is how you tell the controller where that band ends.

lessons.title: Derivative on Measurement
lessons.goal: Take the derivative of the measurement instead of the error and kill the derivative kick.
lessons.theory:
When you change the setpoint by 50 rpm in one sample, the error jumps 50 in one sample, and the raw derivative reports 2500 rpm per second of change that the plant never experienced. `Kd` multiplies that spike and the motor gets a violent kick.

The fix is to notice that in steady setpoint conditions the derivative of the error equals minus the derivative of the measurement. So compute `-(y - y_prev) / dt` instead. Setpoint steps now contribute nothing, while the damping behaviour is unchanged.

Two rows, because one proves nothing. At the setpoint step the measurement has not moved, so the measurement form is computed from two equal readings and returns zero for any `kd` at all, a wrong sign or a `kd` of zero included. Hold the setpoint and let the plant run instead, and the two forms have to land on the same number. That second row is the one that shows the damping survived the change.

This is called **derivative on measurement**, and it should be your default. Almost every industrial PID does it, and almost every hand written Arduino PID does not.

lessons.title: Three Terms, One Command
lessons.goal: Assemble the full PID sum with derivative on measurement and a filter.
lessons.theory:
The full parallel form is `u = Kp*e + Ki*integral(e) + Kd*d`, where `d` is the filtered derivative of the measurement, negated. Three terms answering three questions: where am I now, where have I been, where am I heading.

Written in code the order matters for clarity, not for math: error, integral, derivative, sum, clamp. Any deviation from that order in a code review is a place to look for a bug.

From here the rest of the course is about what wraps around this sum: timing, saturation, feedforward, cascades. The sum itself never gets more complicated than this.
lessons.task: Write `pid_step(state, setpoint, measured, gains, dt)` that updates the dict `state` and returns the command, using derivative on measurement with a filter.

def pid_step(state, setpoint, measured, gains, dt):
    kp, ki, kd, tau_f = gains
    error = setpoint - measured
    state["integral"] = state["integral"] + error * dt
    raw = -(measured - state["last_measured"]) / dt
    alpha = dt / (tau_f + dt)
    state["dfilt"] = state["dfilt"] + alpha * (raw - state["dfilt"])
    u = kp * error + ki * state["integral"] + kd * state["dfilt"]
    state["last_measured"] = measured
    return u

lessons.title: Weighting the Setpoint
lessons.goal: Apply setpoint weighting on the proportional term to soften step responses.
lessons.theory:
Derivative on measurement removed the D kick, but the P term still jumps on a setpoint step. Setpoint weighting softens it: use `Kp * (b * setpoint - measured)` with `b` between 0 and 1.

With `b = 1` you have classic PID. With `b = 0` the proportional term also acts on measurement only, and the setpoint enters the loop exclusively through the integral, which gives a very gentle response with no overshoot and slower tracking.

This single knob is how you get one controller to serve both a smooth setpoint follower and an aggressive disturbance rejecter. Disturbance response does not change with `b` at all, because a disturbance does not touch the setpoint.

lessons.title: Reading a Response Without a Plot
lessons.goal: Classify a response as sluggish, good or ringing from its numbers alone.
lessons.theory:
On a robot you often have a serial log and no plotting tool. Three numbers still tell you what to change: overshoot, number of oscillations before settling, and steady state error.

High overshoot with several swings means too much `Kp` or too little `Kd`. A slow crawl to target with no overshoot means too little `Kp`. A response that reaches the neighbourhood fast and then takes seconds to close the last two percent means too little `Ki`. A slow wide oscillation means too much `Ki`.

Writing that decision tree as code forces you to be precise about the thresholds, and gives you something you can run on real logs later.

lessons.title: The PID Controller Class
lessons.goal: Deliver a production shaped PID class with filter, weighting, limits and reset.
lessons.theory:
This class is the tool for the rest of the course. It holds gains, a derivative filter time, a setpoint weight, output limits and an integral it can clamp. It takes `dt` per call. It has a `reset` that preloads.

Write it once, well, and stop rewriting PID in every project. The number of robots that misbehave because someone retyped the loop from memory at 2 in the morning is not small.

Drive it through a noisy measurement, because that is where most of this class earns its keep. On a clean step the filter time, the integral clamp and the start guard can each be deleted and the final speed still reads 100.0, so one settled number cannot tell a finished controller from a half written one. Put chapter 3 noise on the measurement and count how far the command travels: with no filter at all it moves 312 units of duty across 800 samples, at `tau_f` 0.01 it moves 93, at 0.05 it moves 33, and the speed lands in the same place every time. That travel is heat in the driver and wear in the gearbox. The setpoint weight stays at 1 in this run, which leaves its term an identity, because c3-7 already measured what lowering it buys.

The one thing to leave out is threading. A controller that manages its own timer is a controller you cannot unit test. Give it `dt` and let the caller own the clock.

import random

TAU = 0.35
DT = 0.02
GAIN = 180.0

class PID:
    def __init__(self, kp, ki, kd, tau_f=0.05, b=1.0, out_min=-1.0, out_max=1.0):
        self.kp = kp
        self.ki = ki
        self.kd = kd
        self.tau_f = tau_f
        self.b = b
        self.out_min = out_min
        self.out_max = out_max
        self.integral = 0.0
        self.dfilt = 0.0
        self.last_measured = 0.0
        self.started = False

    def reset(self, current_output=0.0, measured=0.0):
        self.integral = current_output / self.ki if self.ki else 0.0
        self.dfilt = 0.0
        self.last_measured = measured
        self.started = False

    def update(self, setpoint, measured, dt):
        if not self.started:
            self.last_measured = measured
            self.started = True
        error = setpoint - measured
        self.integral = self.integral + error * dt
        if self.ki:
            limit = max(abs(self.out_min), abs(self.out_max)) / self.ki
            self.integral = min(limit, max(-limit, self.integral))
        raw = -(measured - self.last_measured) / dt if dt > 0.0 else 0.0
        alpha = dt / (self.tau_f + dt)
        self.dfilt = self.dfilt + alpha * (raw - self.dfilt)
        self.last_measured = measured
        u = self.kp * (self.b * setpoint - measured) + self.ki * self.integral + self.kd * self.dfilt
        return min(self.out_max, max(self.out_min, u))

def run(tau_f):
    random.seed(7)
    pid = PID(0.01, 0.03, 0.0015, tau_f=tau_f, out_min=0.0, out_max=1.0)
    speed = 0.0
    last = None
    travel = 0.0
    for _ in range(800):
        u = pid.update(100.0, speed + random.uniform(-1.5, 1.5), DT)
        if last is not None:
            travel = travel + abs(u - last)
        last = u
        speed = speed + (GAIN * u - speed) * (DT / TAU) - 8.0 * DT
    return travel, speed

for tau_f in (0.0, 0.01, 0.05):
    travel, speed = run(tau_f)
    print(tau_f, round(travel, 2), round(speed, 3))

lessons.title: The Order of the Knobs
lessons.goal: Follow a manual tuning procedure that converges instead of wandering.
lessons.theory:
Manual tuning works when you change one thing at a time and in the right order. Set `Ki` and `Kd` to zero. Raise `Kp` until the response is fast and slightly oscillatory, then back off by about a third. Add `Ki` until the offset closes in an acceptable time, no faster. Add `Kd` last, only if overshoot still bothers you.

The reason for the order is that each term is fixing a different symptom, and if you start with all three at nonzero you cannot tell which one caused what you are looking at.

Double or halve, never nudge. A 10 percent change to a gain is invisible on a real machine, and you will convince yourself something happened when nothing did.

lessons.title: Finding the Edge
lessons.goal: Measure the ultimate gain and the ultimate period of a plant.

Ziegler-Nichols starts by pushing the loop to the point of sustained oscillation with proportional control only. The gain that produces a steady, non growing swing is the **ultimate gain** `Ku`. The time between two peaks of that swing is the **ultimate period** `Tu`.

On hardware this is a real risk. You are deliberately making the machine unstable, so do it at low setpoints, with limits in place, and with a hand near the power switch. Never do it on an arm that can hit itself.

In simulation you can find it by bisection: raise the gain, check whether the oscillation amplitude grows, and narrow the bracket.

lessons.title: The Closed Loop Table
lessons.goal: Apply the Ziegler-Nichols closed loop rules to turn Ku and Tu into gains.
lessons.theory:
With `Ku` and `Tu` in hand the classic table gives you gains directly. For a PID: `Kp = 0.6*Ku`, `Ti = 0.5*Tu`, `Td = 0.125*Tu`, which converts to `Ki = Kp/Ti` and `Kd = Kp*Td`. For PI: `Kp = 0.45*Ku`, `Ti = Tu/1.2`.

The result is aggressive. Ziegler and Nichols designed for quarter amplitude decay, meaning each oscillation is a quarter of the previous one, and that looks like roughly 25 percent overshoot. Many machines find that unacceptable.

Treat the table as a starting point that is never more than a factor of two wrong, then tune from there. That is genuinely valuable, because a factor of two is a much smaller search space than a blank page.

lessons.title: The Reaction Curve
lessons.goal: Extract dead time and time constant from an open loop step and tune from them.
lessons.theory:
The open loop Ziegler-Nichols method never destabilises the machine. You step the command, log the response, and read two numbers off the curve: the **dead time** `L` before anything moves, and the **time constant** `T` of the rise.

With the process gain `K` equal to the change in output divided by the change in command, the PID rules are `Kp = 1.2*T/(K*L)`, `Ti = 2*L`, `Td = 0.5*L`. Everything hinges on `L`, which is why a plant with almost no dead time gives absurdly high gains and the method quietly fails.

This is the method to use on a heated bed, a chemical bath, or anything you cannot legally make oscillate.

DT = 0.02

def make_trace(steps=600, dead=8, tau=0.35, gain=180.0, duty=0.5):
    y = 0.0
    out = []
    for i in range(steps):
        drive = duty if i >= dead else 0.0
        y = y + (gain * drive - y) * (DT / tau)
        out.append(y)
    return out

def reaction_curve(trace, dt, step_size):
    final = trace[-1]
    k = final / step_size
    best_slope = 0.0
    best_i = 0
    for i in range(1, len(trace)):
        slope = (trace[i] - trace[i - 1]) / dt
        if slope > best_slope:
            best_slope = slope
            best_i = i
    t_at = best_i * dt
    y_at = trace[best_i]
    l = t_at - y_at / best_slope
    t_const = final / best_slope
    return k, max(l, 0.0), t_const

print(tuple(round(v, 3) for v in reaction_curve(make_trace(), DT, 0.5)))
lessons.hint: The tangent crosses zero at `t - y/slope` and reaches the final value at `final/slope` after that.

lessons.title: The Softer Table
lessons.goal: Use the no overshoot and low overshoot variants when 25 percent is unacceptable.
lessons.theory:
Quarter amplitude decay is a choice, not a law. Pessen and others published variants of the same table that trade speed for calm. The **some overshoot** rule uses `Kp = 0.33*Ku`, `Ti = 0.5*Tu`, `Td = 0.33*Tu`. The **no overshoot** rule uses `Kp = 0.2*Ku`, `Ti = 0.5*Tu`, `Td = 0.33*Tu`.

Both keep the same integral and derivative times and simply cut the proportional gain, which is exactly what you would do by hand. Knowing that makes the tables less magical and easier to trust.

On a linear gantry carrying an expensive sensor, no overshoot is not a preference, it is a requirement, and this row of the table is the fastest path to it.

Parallel form uses `Kp`, `Ki`, `Kd`. Standard form uses `Kp`, `Ti`, `Td`, with `Ki = Kp/Ti` and `Kd = Kp*Td`. They describe identical controllers, and every tuning table in the literature is written in one or the other.

Standard form has a real advantage: `Ti` and `Td` are times, so they survive a change of `Kp`. Double the proportional gain in standard form and the integral still repeats the proportional action after the same number of seconds. In parallel form you have to remember to double `Ki` as well.

Most embedded code uses parallel because it is one multiply per term. Convert at the edges, tune in whichever form you think in.

lessons.title: Two Different Jobs
lessons.goal: Score a tune separately for setpoint tracking and for disturbance rejection.
lessons.theory:
A controller tuned to follow setpoints beautifully can be poor at shrugging off a load, and the reverse. They are different tests and they deserve different scores.

Setpoint tracking is what you see in a demo: step the target, look at the response. Disturbance rejection is what matters on a robot in the world: hold the target, apply a load, see how far it sags and how quickly it recovers.

When the two disagree, the setpoint weighting `b` from chapter 3 is the knob that lets you have both. Tune the gains for disturbance rejection, then lower `b` until the setpoint response is calm enough.

lessons.title: What Counts as Better
lessons.goal: Compare tunes with IAE, ISE and ITAE and explain what each one rewards.
lessons.theory:
You cannot optimise a tune without a number. Three classic ones: **IAE** is the integral of the absolute error, **ISE** squares the error so it punishes big deviations hard, and **ITAE** multiplies by elapsed time so it punishes errors that persist.

They lead to different tunes. ISE gives fast aggressive controllers that tolerate a long low amplitude tail. ITAE gives calm controllers that refuse to leave a residual offset. IAE sits between them and is the safest default.

Pick one before you start comparing, and write it down. Switching criteria mid tuning is how people spend a day going in circles.

lessons.title: The Relay Trick
lessons.goal: Find Ku and Tu automatically with relay feedback instead of raising Kp by hand.
lessons.theory:
The relay method replaces the controller with a bang bang switch of amplitude `d`: full positive when the error is positive, full negative when it is negative. Any plant with enough phase lag will settle into a limit cycle at exactly its ultimate frequency.

Measure the amplitude `a` of that cycle and its period, and the describing function gives `Ku = 4*d / (pi*a)` and `Tu` equal to the measured period. You now have Ziegler-Nichols inputs without ever running an unstable controller.

This is what the autotune button on a temperature controller does. It is bounded, repeatable and safe enough to run on a real machine, which is why it is worth having in your own code.

import math
TAU = 0.35
DT = 0.02
GAIN = 180.0
DELAY = 3

def relay_autotune(d=0.3, setpoint=100.0, steps=3000):
    speed = 0.0
    pipe = [0.0] * DELAY
    peaks = []
    crossings = []
    prev_error = setpoint
    for step in range(steps):
        error = setpoint - speed
        u = 0.5 + d if error > 0.0 else 0.5 - d
        pipe.append(u)
        speed = speed + (GAIN * pipe.pop(0) - speed) * (DT / TAU)
        if step > 800:
            if error > 0.0 and prev_error <= 0.0:
                crossings.append(step)
            peaks.append(speed)
        prev_error = error
    if len(crossings) < 2 or not peaks:
        return 0.0, 0.0
    amplitude = 0.5 * (max(peaks) - min(peaks))
    period = (crossings[-1] - crossings[0]) / (len(crossings) - 1) * DT
    ku = 4.0 * d / (math.pi * amplitude)
    return ku, period

print(tuple(round(v, 4) for v in relay_autotune()))
lessons.hint: Amplitude is half the peak to peak swing, and the period is the average spacing between rising crossings.

lessons.title: The Tick That Defines Everything
lessons.goal: Run a loop on a fixed period and understand what dt means to your gains.
lessons.theory:
Every discrete controller assumes a sample period. Change it and the meaning of `Ki` and `Kd` changes with it, unless you multiply and divide by the real `dt` as this course has been doing.

Even with a correct `dt`, the loop rate is not free to choose. Too slow and the controller reacts to a world that has already moved on. Too fast and you burn CPU, amplify noise, and gain nothing because the plant cannot respond that quickly.

On a Raspberry Pi 4 a motor speed loop typically runs at 100 to 200 Hz. A balancing angle loop wants 200 to 500 Hz. A heated bed is happy at 1 Hz.

lessons.solution:
import time

def fixed_rate(period, iterations, body):
    periods = []
    next_tick = time.perf_counter()
    last = next_tick
    for i in range(iterations):
        next_tick = next_tick + period
        delay = next_tick - time.perf_counter()
        if delay > 0.0:
            time.sleep(delay)
        now = time.perf_counter()
        periods.append(now - last)
        last = now
        body(i)
    return periods

print(len(fixed_rate(0.002, 20, lambda i: None)))
lessons.hint: Advance `next_tick` by the fixed period, never by the current time, or the error accumulates.

lessons.title: How Fast Is Fast Enough
lessons.goal: Pick a sample rate from the plant time constant instead of guessing.
lessons.theory:
The working rule is to sample 10 to 20 times faster than the closed loop time constant you want. If you need the wheel to reach speed in 200 ms, sample at least every 10 to 20 ms.

Sampling faster than that stops helping. The plant cannot respond, so the extra samples only give the derivative more noise to amplify and the integral more chances to accumulate quantisation.

The other bound comes from the actuator. A brushed motor driven at 20 kHz PWM has an electrical response far faster than the loop, so the loop is free. A hobby servo that only accepts a new pulse every 20 ms caps you at 50 Hz no matter what the code can do.
lessons.task: Write `choose_rate(tau_closed)` returning a recommended period as the closed loop time constant divided by 15, rounded down to a multiple of 1 ms, with a floor of 1 ms.
lessons.hint: Convert to milliseconds with `int`, clamp to at least 1, then convert back.

lessons.title: The Signal That Lies
lessons.goal: Reproduce aliasing by sampling a fast oscillation too slowly.
lessons.theory:
Sample a 30 Hz vibration at 25 Hz and you will not see 30 Hz. You will see a slow 5 Hz wave that does not exist, and your controller will dutifully fight it. The false frequency is the distance from the real one to the nearest multiple of the sample rate.

This is **aliasing**, and it is why a robot with a stiff gearbox can develop a slow wobble that no gain change fixes. The wobble is a sampling artefact of a mechanical resonance you never intended to measure.

Pick the demonstration rate with care. Sampling that same 30 Hz at exactly 20 Hz puts the alias at 10 Hz, which is exactly half the sample rate, and every sample lands on a zero crossing of the sine. The sequence comes out as floating point dust around 1e-14 and looks like nothing at all rather than like a slow wave.

The cure is a low pass filter in front of the sampler, analog if the sensor allows it, or a much faster inner sampling with averaging if it does not. Filtering after the fact does not help: the false frequency is already indistinguishable from a real one.
lessons.task: Sample a 30 Hz sine at 25 Hz and at 400 Hz, and print how many sign changes each sampled sequence contains over one second.
lessons.hint: Sample time is the index divided by the rate, and the sine argument is `2*pi*f*t`.

lessons.title: The Clock That Wanders
lessons.goal: Measure real jitter and pass the actual dt into the controller.
lessons.theory:
A Python loop on Linux does not tick perfectly. Garbage collection, a busy USB bus, another process, and your 5 ms period becomes 5.3 ms, then 4.8, then once in a while 19 ms because something blocked.

A controller that assumes a constant `dt` sees that as a change in gain. The integral under accumulates, the derivative spikes, and the loop gets a small kick every time the system hiccups.

The fix costs nothing: measure the actual elapsed time and pass it in. Every `update` in this course already takes `dt` for exactly this reason. Clamp it too, because a 19 ms sample after a stall should not be allowed to inject a huge integral step.

The function hands back the new last time so the caller can carry it into the next call. Throw that half away and rebuild `last_time` from `now` yourself, and every gap you measure is the period you assumed rather than the one that happened.

lessons.title: The Loop That Missed Its Turn
lessons.goal: Detect an overrun and decide what the controller does about it.
lessons.theory:
Sooner or later the loop body takes longer than the period. What the controller does next is a design decision, not an accident.

Skipping the sample entirely is usually wrong, because the plant kept moving. Running immediately with the true, larger `dt` is usually right, because the integral and derivative are computed correctly for the time that actually passed. Catching up by running several iterations back to back is almost always wrong, because it floods the actuator.

What you must never do is silently ignore it. Count overruns, expose the count, and if it rises above a few per thousand your loop rate is a lie and the gains you tuned no longer apply.

lessons.title: The Incremental Form
lessons.goal: Implement velocity form PID, which computes a change in output rather than an output.
lessons.theory:
The **velocity form** computes `du` instead of `u`: `du = Kp*(e - e_prev) + Ki*e*dt + Kd*(e - 2*e_prev + e_prev2)/dt`, and the actuator command is `u = u_prev + du`.

It has two practical advantages. There is no explicit integral to wind up, because the accumulation lives in the actuator's own state, and switching between manual and automatic is naturally bumpless since you always start from the current output.

It is the natural form when the actuator itself integrates, like a stepper receiving step pulses or a valve driven by a motor. It is a poor fit when the actuator is a plain duty cycle you must write in full every sample.

lessons.title: Small Numbers, Big Problems
lessons.goal: Show how float accumulation and integer truncation corrupt a slow integral.
lessons.theory:
An integral that adds `e * dt` with `dt` at 0.001 and `e` near zero is adding numbers around 1e-6 to a total that may be in the hundreds. In 32 bit floats, common on a microcontroller, those additions can vanish entirely.

The symptom is a loop that never quite closes the last fraction of a percent, and no amount of `Ki` fixes it because the term being added is below the resolution of the sum.

The remedy that always pays is to accumulate in a wider type. Rescaling the accumulator into larger units is a fixed point trick and does not carry over: in floating point every magnitude is stored with the same relative precision, so accumulating the raw error and multiplying by `dt` at the end loses just as much as the naive sum, and which of the two lands closer on a given run is luck rather than design. Widening the accumulator turns a tenth of a percent of drift into a part in ten billion.

lessons.hint: Python floats are already 64 bit. Write the same sum as `naive` and simply do not route it through `to_f32`.

lessons.title: The Discrete PID, Timed Honestly
lessons.goal: Combine measured dt, overrun detection and the PID class into one runnable loop.
lessons.theory:
Everything in this chapter lands in one function: a loop that keeps its own schedule, measures the real elapsed time, clamps it, feeds it to the controller, counts overruns, and stops cleanly.

This is what a control task looks like on a Raspberry Pi before you move it to a microcontroller. The structure does not change when you port it; only the sleep and the sensor read do.

Run it twice, because a counter that never counts is not evidence. On a plant that answers at once the loop keeps its 2 ms schedule and the overrun branch never runs, so a count of zero cannot tell a working detector from one wired to nothing. Give the same loop a sensor read that blocks for 3 ms and the period is impossible: every tick after the first slips, and the count goes from none of a hundred to all but one of forty odd. Print the tick total beside the count, because the count alone means nothing without it, and expect both to differ a little on every run. This is the first loop in the course whose numbers come from a real clock instead of a fixed step.

Build it now, because chapter 9 asks you to run a balancing controller inside exactly this skeleton.

lessons.title: The Ceiling and the Floor
lessons.goal: Model actuator saturation and see the loop become nonlinear at the limits.
lessons.theory:
A TB6612FNG driving a 12 V gearmotor can deliver a duty between minus one and one, and not a bit more. Your controller can ask for 3.4 all it likes.

The instant the command hits a limit, the loop stops being linear. Feedback is broken while saturated: the plant no longer responds to changes in the controller output, because the output is not changing. Every intuition built on linear analysis is suspended until the command comes back inside the range.

This is why saturation deserves its own chapter. It is not a detail at the edges, it is the regime a robot actually operates in every time it starts, stops or hits something.

lessons.title: Conditional Integration
lessons.goal: Stop the integral from growing while the actuator is saturated in the same direction.
lessons.theory:
The simplest correct anti windup rule: keep accumulating only when the actuator is not saturated, or when the new error would push the command back inside the range.

That second half is what separates it from a blunt freeze. If the output is pinned at maximum and the error goes negative, integrating is exactly what you want, because it unwinds the accumulator.

Do not take that on faith, because from a cold accumulator the two rules are indistinguishable. Conditional integration stops the integral the instant the command clips, so ki times the integral never climbs far enough above the limit to hold the command pinned once the error changes sign. The push back half fires zero times, and a blunt freeze prints the same numbers.

The difference appears when the loop inherits an accumulator already wound past the limit: a handover, a retune that raises ki, or a stretch that ran unprotected. There the blunt freeze is saturated forever, so it never integrates again and parks the command at maximum. The conditional rule unwinds it and the loop recovers.

So run both starts, and print the accumulator beside the error, because the error on its own cannot tell them apart. A loop parked at full duty reads 60 rpm short whatever the reason, since 60 is only the plant ceiling of 180 minus the setpoint, and a student cannot see from it whether the rule never recovered or the plant simply ran out of top end. The accumulator is the honest witness. The blunt freeze ends holding exactly WOUND, untouched since the first clipped sample, while the conditional rule ends on the value that actually holds the setpoint, ki times it being the duty the plant needs.

lessons.title: Back Calculation
lessons.goal: Implement back calculation anti windup and tune its tracking time constant.
lessons.theory:
Back calculation feeds the clipped amount back into the accumulator: `integral += (u_clamped - u_raw) / Tt`, where `Tt` is the tracking time constant.

Unlike a hard freeze it degrades gracefully. The deeper the saturation, the harder the accumulator is pulled back, so the controller is always ready to leave the limit at roughly the right value. A common choice is `Tt` equal to the square root of `Ti * Td`, or simply `Ti` when there is no derivative.

Measure it on the way down, not on the way up. While the actuator is pinned the speed sits at the plant's ceiling no matter what `Tt` you chose, so the peak reached during saturation is the same number for every tuning and for none at all. What anti windup buys shows up after the setpoint drops: how long the machine keeps running above the new target before the accumulator has unwound enough to let go.

This is what most industrial PID blocks implement, and it is worth the four extra lines on any robot whose actuator saturates during normal motion, which is all of them.

DT = 0.02
GAIN = 180.0

def run(setpoints, tt, kp=0.004, ki=0.02):
    speed = 0.0
    integral = 0.0
    previous = setpoints[0]
    counting = False
    recovery = 0
    for setpoint in setpoints:
        if setpoint < previous:
            counting = True
        previous = setpoint
        error = setpoint - speed
        raw = kp * error + ki * integral
        duty = min(1.0, max(0.0, raw))
        integral = integral + error * DT
        integral = integral + (duty - raw) / tt * DT / ki
        speed = speed + (GAIN * duty - speed) * (DT / TAU)
        if counting:
            if speed <= setpoint:
                counting = False
            else:
                recovery = recovery + 1
    return recovery

    print(tt, run(profile, tt))

lessons.title: The Zone Where Nothing Happens
lessons.goal: Model a dead zone from static friction and measure the resulting steady state error.
lessons.theory:
Command a gearmotor at 4 percent duty and it does not turn. Static friction in the gearbox and the motor's own cogging swallow the torque. Somewhere around 12 to 18 percent it breaks free, and once it is turning that same slice of duty keeps being eaten for as long as it turns.

That is the **dead zone**: below the threshold nothing moves at all, and above it the wheel behaves as though every command arrived `DEAD` smaller than you sent it. Model it that way and a compensator can undo it, which is the next lesson.

It breaks proportional control exactly where you want the machine to be gentle. A P loop asking for a slow speed asks for a small duty, and a small duty is precisely what the friction swallows, so the loop stops short and stays there with the error frozen. Raising `Kp` does not fix it honestly, it only moves the speed at which the loop runs out of authority.
lessons.task: Add a dead zone of 0.15 to the plant, run the same P loop at a 20 rpm request against the plant with and without it, and print the speed each one settles at.
lessons.hint: Compare the absolute value of the duty against `DEAD`. Below it there is no drive at all, and above it subtract `DEAD` in whichever direction the duty points.

lessons.title: Jumping the Gap
lessons.goal: Compensate the dead zone by offsetting the command past the breakaway threshold.
lessons.theory:
If you know the motor needs 0.15 duty before it moves, add it. The compensator maps a requested command `u` into `sign(u) * (dead + (1 - dead) * |u|)`, so a request of zero stays zero and any nonzero request lands above the threshold, where the plant subtracts the same `dead` back out and the pair very nearly cancels.

This is feedforward applied to a nonlinearity rather than to a load, and it is remarkably effective. On the previous lesson's plant a 20 rpm request left the wheel completely stationary, because the duty the loop asked for never cleared the threshold. With the compensator in front, the same loop settles at 7.59 rpm against the 8.37 rpm it reaches on a frictionless plant. What is left is ordinary proportional droop, not friction.

Measure `dead` per motor, not per model. Two units off the same reel can differ by 30 percent, and the value drifts as bearings wear in.
lessons.task: Write `compensate(u, dead)` implementing that mapping, apply it before the plant from the previous lesson, and print the speed the loop settles at without the compensator and with it.
lessons.hint: Keep the sign separate, scale the magnitude into the range above the dead zone, and special case exactly zero.

lessons.title: The Thermostat's Wisdom
lessons.goal: Implement bang bang control with hysteresis and compute its switching frequency.
lessons.theory:
Not every actuator is proportional. A relay driving a 200 W heater is on or off, and the controller must be too. Bang bang with a **hysteresis** band turns on below `setpoint - h`, turns off above `setpoint + h`, and does nothing in between.

Without the band, the relay chatters: it switches every time noise crosses the threshold, which on a mechanical relay means a few million cycles and a welded contact. The band buys switch life at the price of a temperature that ripples across `2h`.

The same pattern appears anywhere the actuator has a switching cost: a solenoid valve, a cooling fan, a contactor on a big motor.
lessons.task: Write a `Hysteresis` class with `setpoint`, `band` and `update(measured)` returning True or False, and count the switches over a noisy run.

import random

class Hysteresis:
    def __init__(self, setpoint, band):
        self.setpoint = setpoint
        self.band = band
        self.on = False

lessons.title: Chatter and Its Cure
lessons.goal: Add hysteresis to a direction change and stop a motor from buzzing around zero.
lessons.theory:
The same chatter appears in a proportional loop the moment the command crosses zero and the H bridge must reverse. Noise around zero makes the bridge flip direction hundreds of times a second, which produces heat, audible buzz and current spikes.

The fix is the same idea applied to direction rather than to on and off: require the command to exceed a small threshold before allowing a reversal, and hold the previous direction inside the band.

Combine this with the dead zone compensation from earlier and a wheel that used to sit buzzing at its target sits silent instead.
lessons.task: Write a `DirectionGuard` class holding the last direction, with `update(u, band)` returning zero inside the band unless the direction is unchanged.
lessons.hint: A reversal is a request whose sign differs from the stored direction; block it while the magnitude is small.

lessons.title: Slew, the Other Limit
lessons.goal: Rate limit the command and see how it protects mechanics and current draw.
lessons.theory:
Actuators have a second limit that is easy to forget: how fast the command may change. Slamming a motor command from zero to full in one 5 ms sample draws a stall current spike, shocks the gearbox teeth, and on a robot arm makes the whole frame ring.

A **slew rate limiter** caps the change per sample at `rate * dt`. It is one line, and on a robot with plastic gears it is the difference between a machine that lasts and one that strips a gear in a week.

Be aware it adds lag, and lag costs stability margin. Set the rate as high as the mechanics tolerate, not as low as looks smooth.
lessons.task: Write a `SlewLimiter` class with `rate` in units per second and `update(target, dt)`, and print how many samples a zero to one step takes at 4 per second.
lessons.hint: Clamp the difference, not the target, so the limiter works in both directions. Put that difference in a local called `delta`, clamp it to plus or minus the per sample `step`, then add it to the stored value.

lessons.title: The Guarded Controller
lessons.goal: Combine saturation, anti windup, dead zone compensation and slew into one output stage.
lessons.theory:
All the protections in this chapter belong in one place: an output stage that sits between the PID sum and the driver. Slew limit first, then dead zone compensation, then saturation, then report the delivered value back to the controller for anti windup.

The order matters. Compensating the dead zone after clamping would push the command back outside the range. Anti windup must see the value actually delivered, not the value requested before compensation.

Get this stage right once and every controller you write afterwards inherits it.

Watch `saturated` flip both ways before you trust it. The slew limiter stands in front of the clamp, so a short burst of demand walks the output up a fraction at a time and never reaches the bound. A stage that reports False on every sample has not been tested, it has only been run.

lessons.title: The Model Speaks First
lessons.goal: Separate feedforward from feedback and explain what each one is responsible for.
lessons.theory:
Feedback is reactive. It cannot act until an error exists, which means every disturbance costs you at least one error before it is corrected.

**Feedforward** uses a model of the plant to compute the command the setpoint requires, before any error appears. The feedback loop is then left to clean up the difference between the model and reality, which is small.

The model below is deliberately wrong, as every bench measurement of a real motor is: it believes the plant gain is 190 when it is 180. That five percent is exactly what the P term has left to clean up, and the number it leaves behind is the honest measure of the pair. Compare the error each configuration settles at rather than the largest error either one ever saw, because the largest error of a step from rest is the step itself and both configurations start there.

Saying it plainly: feedforward does the work, feedback fixes the mistakes. On a well modelled axis, 90 percent of the command comes from feedforward and the PID barely moves. That is a sign of a good design, not a lazy one.

lessons.title: The Motor Curve
lessons.goal: Fit Ks and Kv from measured duty and speed pairs.
lessons.theory:
A DC motor at steady speed obeys `duty = Ks * sign(v) + Kv * v` closely enough for control. `Ks` is the static term that overcomes friction, `Kv` is the slope of duty against speed.

You measure them by sweeping duty in steps, letting the wheel settle at each, and logging the pairs. A least squares fit on the nonzero points gives both constants in a minute of bench work.

This is the single highest value hour you can spend on a drivebase. Two constants per motor turn a twitchy PID into a loop that mostly rides on feedforward and hardly needs tuning.
lessons.task: Write `fit_ks_kv(samples)` doing a least squares fit of `duty = ks + kv * speed` over the samples with positive speed, and print the constants.
lessons.starter:
def fit_ks_kv(samples):
    # TODO: drop the stalled samples, then least squares slope and intercept of duty against speed
    return 0.0, 0.0

samples = [(0.0, 0.0), (20.0, 0.22), (40.0, 0.30), (60.0, 0.38), (90.0, 0.50), (120.0, 0.62), (150.0, 0.74)]
ks, kv = fit_ks_kv(samples)
print(round(ks, 4), round(kv, 6))
lessons.solution:
def fit_ks_kv(samples):
    rows = [(speed, duty) for speed, duty in samples if speed > 0.0]
    n = len(rows)
    sx = sum(s for s, _ in rows)
    sy = sum(d for _, d in rows)
    sxx = sum(s * s for s, _ in rows)
    sxy = sum(s * d for s, d in rows)
    denom = n * sxx - sx * sx
    if denom == 0.0:
        return 0.0, 0.0
    kv = (n * sxy - sx * sy) / denom
    ks = (sy - kv * sx) / n
    return ks, kv

samples = [(0.0, 0.0), (20.0, 0.22), (40.0, 0.30), (60.0, 0.38), (90.0, 0.50), (120.0, 0.62), (150.0, 0.74)]
ks, kv = fit_ks_kv(samples)
print(round(ks, 4), round(kv, 6))

Accumulate the four sums into lowercase locals `sx`, `sy`, `sxx` and `sxy`, put the shared denominator `n * sxx - sx * sx` into `denom` so you can guard it against zero, and the slope is then `(n * sxy - sx * sy) / denom` with the intercept following from it.

lessons.title: The Cost of Changing Speed
lessons.goal: Add an acceleration feedforward term and use it during a ramp.
lessons.theory:
`Ks` and `Kv` describe steady state. While the wheel is accelerating, extra torque is needed to overcome inertia, and that term is proportional to the commanded acceleration: `duty += Ka * a`.

Without it, every ramp lags: the feedback loop has to build an error before it supplies the extra push. With it, the wheel follows the ramp almost exactly and the PID output stays near zero throughout.

A ramp is only a ramp while the actuator can still deliver it. This plant needs `target / 180 + 0.35 * slope / 180` of duty to stay on a ramp, so at 200 rpm per second it runs out of duty a little past 110 rpm. Ask it for more and every value of `Ka` measures the same saturation, which is a fact about the motor and not about the tuning. Keep the ramp inside what the plant can do, half a second here, and the term is measurable.

`Ka` is harder to measure than `Kv`. The practical method is to run a known ramp, look at the residual PID output, and raise `Ka` until that residual is flat. Its ideal value is the plant time constant over the plant gain, 0.35 over 180, which is where the 0.0019 below comes from.

def ramp_error(ka, ks=0.02, kv=1.0 / 180.0, kp=0.004, steps=25, slope=200.0):

    target = 0.0

lessons.title: Two Sources, One Command
lessons.goal: Sum feedforward and PID correctly, including what anti windup must see.
lessons.theory:
The combined command is `u = ff(setpoint) + pid(error)`. Simple, with two traps.

First, the saturation limits apply to the sum, not to the PID alone. If feedforward already asks for 0.95, the PID has 0.05 of room and its integral must know that, or it winds up against a ceiling it cannot see.

Second, when feedforward is good, the PID gains you tuned without it are now too high, because the loop is being asked to do far less. Retune after adding feedforward, always downward.
lessons.task: Write `combined(ff_value, pid_value, low, high)` returning the clamped sum and the amount clipped, and feed that clipped amount to back calculation.
lessons.hint: The clipped amount is the delivered value minus the raw sum, which is zero when nothing was clipped.

lessons.title: The Encoder Speaks
lessons.goal: Decode quadrature signals into a signed count.
lessons.theory:
A quadrature encoder gives two square waves, A and B, 90 degrees apart. The order in which they change tells you direction; the number of changes tells you distance.

Decoding in software means looking at the previous AB pair and the current one. Of the sixteen possible transitions, four mean forward, four mean backward, four mean nothing changed, and four are impossible and indicate a missed sample.

Print the direction totals apart rather than added together. A forward run of five and a backward run of four summed into a single 1 would look exactly the same as a decoder with the sign inverted, or one counting half the edges, so the sum on its own proves nothing about the table.

Counting all four transitions per cycle is called 4x decoding and gives four times the resolution of counting rising edges on A alone. On a 12 CPR motor that is the difference between 12 and 48 counts per motor revolution.
lessons.task: Write `quad_step(prev_ab, ab)` returning 1, -1 or 0 using a lookup table, and run it over a forward sequence, a backward sequence and a glitched one, printing the three totals separately so direction and rejection are both visible.
lessons.hint: Eight valid transitions go in the table; everything else, including a pair that did not change, falls back to zero.

lessons.title: From Counts to Radians
lessons.goal: Convert encoder counts into a velocity in physical units.
lessons.theory:
Counts per sample is not a unit anyone can reason about. Convert once, at the boundary, and keep the whole controller in physical units.

For a motor with `cpr` counts per output revolution, angular velocity is `counts / cpr * 2*pi / dt` radians per second, or `counts / cpr / dt * 60` rpm. For a wheel of radius `r`, linear speed is that angular velocity multiplied by `r`.

Getting these conversions in one function, with the constants named after the actual hardware, is what makes gains transferable between the simulator and the robot.
lessons.task: Write `EncoderVelocity` with `cpr` and `wheel_radius`, plus `update(self, counts, dt)` returning a tuple of rad/s, rpm and m/s.
lessons.solution:
import math

class EncoderVelocity:
    def __init__(self, cpr, wheel_radius):
        self.cpr = cpr
        self.wheel_radius = wheel_radius

    def update(self, counts, dt):
        if dt <= 0.0:
            return 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
        revs = counts / self.cpr
        rad_s = revs * 2.0 * math.pi / dt
        rpm = revs / dt * 60.0
        m_s = rad_s * self.wheel_radius
        return rad_s, rpm, m_s

print(tuple(round(v, 4) for v in e.update(34, 0.02)))
lessons.hint: Compute the revolutions in `revs` first, then `rad_s` from it, and the rpm and the m/s from those two.

lessons.title: Smoothing Without Lying
lessons.goal: Filter a velocity estimate and quantify the lag the filter adds.
lessons.theory:
A raw velocity from counts is noisy, so everyone filters it. What most people forget is that a filter with time constant `tau_f` delays the estimate by roughly `tau_f`, and the controller is now steering with old information.

That delay eats stability margin exactly like transport delay does. A heavy filter on the feedback path is one of the most common reasons a loop that looks fine on paper oscillates on the bench.

The useful discipline is to state the lag out loud. If your filter has a 40 ms time constant and your loop wanted a 100 ms response, you have spent 40 percent of your budget on smoothing.

lessons.title: Closing the Velocity Loop
lessons.goal: Build a complete velocity controller with feedforward, PI feedback and the output stage.
lessons.theory:
This is the workhorse of every wheeled robot: a velocity loop per motor, running at 100 to 200 Hz, taking a target in rpm and producing a duty.

The structure is now fixed. Read counts, convert to rpm, filter, compute feedforward from the target, compute PI on the error, sum, pass through the output stage, apply anti windup with whatever was clipped.

The settled speed will not show you any of this. Build the same class with the feedforward gains at zero and it still lands on 100.0, because that is the integral's job and the integral gets there either way. What the feedforward changes is how much work is left for the feedback: with it, the accumulator ends at 0.144, and without it the accumulator has to carry the whole steady command and ends at 11.656, eighty times larger. The trip is shorter too, 0.24 seconds to ninety percent against 0.32. Print the accumulator and the rise, not just the destination.

With `Ks`, `Kv` and `Ka` measured, the PI gains end up small and the loop is forgiving. That is the payoff for the bench work in this chapter.

lessons.solution:
TAU = 0.35
DT = 0.01
GAIN = 180.0

class VelocityController:
    def __init__(self, ks, kv, kp, ki, tt=0.2):
        self.ks = ks
        self.kv = kv
        self.kp = kp
        self.ki = ki
        self.tt = tt
        self.integral = 0.0

    def update(self, target, measured, dt):
        sign = 1.0 if target > 0.0 else (-1.0 if target < 0.0 else 0.0)
        ff = self.ks * sign + self.kv * target
        error = target - measured
        self.integral = self.integral + error * dt
        raw = ff + self.kp * error + self.ki * self.integral
        delivered = min(1.0, max(0.0, raw))
        if self.ki:
            self.integral = self.integral + (delivered - raw) / self.tt * dt / self.ki
        return delivered

def run(ks, kv):
    c = VelocityController(ks, kv, 0.004, 0.05)
    speed = 0.0
    below = 0
    for _ in range(3000):
        speed = speed + (GAIN * c.update(100.0, speed, DT) - speed) * (DT / TAU) - 14.0 * DT
        if speed < 90.0:
            below = below + 1
    return below * DT, c.integral, speed

for ks, kv in ((0.0, 0.0), (0.02, 1.0 / 180.0)):
    rise, integral, speed = run(ks, kv)
    print(ks, round(rise, 2), round(integral, 3), round(speed, 3))

lessons.title: The Profile Feeds the Loop
lessons.goal: Generate a trapezoidal velocity profile and use it as a moving setpoint.
lessons.theory:
Handing a velocity loop a step from 0 to 150 rpm asks for infinite acceleration, and the loop responds by saturating. Handing it a **trapezoidal profile**, which ramps up at a fixed acceleration, cruises, then ramps down, asks for something the motor can actually deliver.

The profile also gives you the acceleration to feed the `Ka` term, which is the other half of why profiles make tracking so much better than steps.

Every motion controller in a CNC, a 3D printer or a robot arm generates profiles like this. The controller does not follow a destination, it follows a plan.

    out = []
    ramp_time = v_max / accel
    t = 0.0
    while t < total_time:
        # TODO: ramp up, hold, and start slowing down in time to arrive
        out.append((0.0, 0.0))
        t = t + dt

profile = trapezoid(150.0, 300.0, 2.0, 0.01)
print(len(profile), profile[10], profile[100], profile[-5])
lessons.solution:
def trapezoid(v_max, accel, total_time, dt):
    out = []
    ramp_time = v_max / accel
    t = 0.0
    while t < total_time:
        if t < ramp_time:
            v = accel * t
            a = accel
        elif t > total_time - ramp_time:
            v = accel * max(0.0, total_time - t)
            a = -accel
        else:
            v = v_max
            a = 0.0
        out.append((min(v, v_max), a))

lessons.title: The Plant That Integrates
lessons.goal: Control position, where the plant integrates the command, and see why Ki is rarely needed.
lessons.theory:
A velocity loop controls a plant that settles at a speed. A position loop controls a plant that keeps moving as long as the command is nonzero, because position is the integral of velocity.

That integration is already inside the plant, so the loop has what control engineers call type 1 behaviour: a constant setpoint is tracked with zero steady state error using proportional control alone. Adding `Ki` to a position loop is usually a way to add overshoot for no benefit.

Run it long enough to be steady, and run it twice. With the joint free the error goes to zero at every gain, which is the whole claim, and a short run hides it: at 600 samples the softest gain still reads 6.38 counts short, and the table then looks like the droop of chapter 1 and teaches the opposite of this lesson. Against a constant DRIFT the droop is real, and it is the gain that sets it, at DRIFT divided by SPEED_PER_DUTY times `kp`.

The exception is a persistent force, like gravity on an arm or a spring on a gripper. Then you need either an integral or, better, a feedforward that knows about the force.
