lessons.title: Damping the Arm
lessons.goal: Use PD on position and show why the D term is doing the work of a shock absorber.
lessons.theory:
A position plant with any inertia rings under pure proportional control, because the mass carries past the target. The derivative term is the damper: it produces a command opposing the current velocity.

That interpretation is exact. On a position loop, the derivative of the error is minus the velocity, so `Kd` is literally a velocity feedback gain, and PD position control is the same thing as a spring plus damper in mechanical terms. `Kp` is the spring stiffness, `Kd` is the damping coefficient.

Print the overshoot, not the peak position. The two differ by the whole setpoint, and at the damped end the peak lands so close to the target that at two decimals it prints as the target itself, where a reader cannot tell an arm that never crossed from one that was clipped there. Read as overshoot at four decimals that last row is 0.0048, a crossing that really happened and really was measured, and the series 60.0394, 30.7946, 6.9356, 0.0048 is the damper closing the gap. The duty limit in the code does bite while the arm accelerates, on 122 samples at `kd` zero and 21 at 0.008, but it is not what produces that last number: take the limit away and it reads 0.0049.

Once you see it that way, tuning a robot joint stops being trial and error. You are choosing how stiff and how damped you want the joint to feel.

lessons.title: A Loop Inside a Loop
lessons.goal: Build a cascade where a position controller commands a velocity controller.
lessons.theory:
**Cascade control** puts a fast inner loop inside a slow outer one. The outer position controller does not command duty, it commands a target velocity. The inner velocity controller turns that into duty.

The payoff is disturbance rejection. A load that slows the wheel is caught by the inner loop within a few milliseconds, long before the position error grows enough for the outer loop to notice.

Neither claim shows up in the final position, which is 90 whatever you do, because the outer loop is an integrator that gets there in the end even from a badly tuned inner loop, and it would read 90 with the outer loop bypassed too. Ask the cascade two questions it can only answer if both loops are real. The first is the peak speed it allowed itself: clamping the inner setpoint hands you a speed limit for free, so a 40 limit peaks at exactly 40.0 and a 120 limit at 119.5, while a 250 limit peaks at 200.89 because by then the clamp has stopped binding and you are reading the plant instead. The second is how many times the position crosses the target on its way to rest.

The rule that makes cascades work is separation of speed: the inner loop must be roughly five to ten times faster than the outer one. Violate it and the two loops fight, producing a ringing that neither one alone would show: with the inner loop at 60 ms, an outer gain of 3 reaches the target without crossing it once, 12 rings through it 13 times and 30 rings 21 times. The ringing does die out, and the counts are the same after 6 seconds and after 60, so what the gain buys you is a worse trip, not an unstable one.
lessons.task: Write `cascade(kp_pos, inner)` where the outer loop produces a velocity target clamped to a maximum and the inner velocity loop produces the duty, returning the final position, the peak velocity and how many times the position crossed the target. Print the peak velocity for three inner setpoint limits, then the crossings for three outer gains.

DT = 0.005
TAU_V = 0.06
SPEED_MAX = 220.0

def cascade(kp_pos, kp_v, ki_v, target=90.0, steps=1200, v_limit=180.0):
    position = 0.0
    velocity = 0.0
    integral = 0.0
    v_peak = 0.0
    crossings = 0

lessons.solution:
DT = 0.005
TAU_V = 0.06
SPEED_MAX = 220.0

def cascade(kp_pos, kp_v, ki_v, target=90.0, steps=1200, v_limit=180.0):
    position = 0.0
    velocity = 0.0
    integral = 0.0
    v_peak = 0.0
    crossings = 0
    for _ in range(steps):
        v_target = kp_pos * (target - position)
        v_target = min(v_limit, max(-v_limit, v_target))
        error = v_target - velocity
        integral = integral + error * DT
        duty = min(1.0, max(-1.0, kp_v * error + ki_v * integral))
        velocity = velocity + (SPEED_MAX * duty - velocity) * (DT / TAU_V)
        previous = position
        position = position + velocity * DT
        if (position - target) * (previous - target) < 0.0:
            crossings = crossings + 1
        v_peak = max(v_peak, velocity)
    return position, v_peak, crossings

for limit in (40.0, 120.0, 250.0):
    print(limit, round(cascade(3.0, 0.004, 0.06, v_limit=limit)[1], 2))
for kp_pos in (3.0, 12.0, 30.0):
    print(kp_pos, cascade(kp_pos, 0.004, 0.06)[2])

lessons.title: Holding Up the Weight
lessons.goal: Add gravity compensation to an arm and remove the offset the integral was hiding.
lessons.theory:
A robot arm at 40 degrees from horizontal needs a constant torque just to not fall. Without compensation the PID supplies it through the integral, slowly, and the arm sags every time it moves to a new angle.

Gravity compensation computes that torque from the model: `u_g = Kg * cos(theta)`, where `theta` is measured from horizontal and `Kg` is the command needed to hold the arm out straight.

One constant, measured by finding the duty that holds the arm level, and the arm stops sagging at every angle. This is feedforward for a known force, and it is why serious arm code always carries a model of its own mass.

lessons.title: The Thing That Wants to Fall
lessons.goal: Simulate an inverted pendulum and see why it needs feedback to exist at all.
lessons.theory:
A pendulum hanging down is stable: push it and it returns. A pendulum standing up is **unstable**: the further it tips, the harder gravity pulls it over. There is no open loop command that keeps it upright.

The linearised model near vertical is `theta_ddot = (g/l) * theta - (1/l) * a_cart`, where `a_cart` is the horizontal acceleration of the base. The positive sign on the first term is the instability, in one symbol.

The second term is the lever you have. Accelerate the base toward the direction of the fall and the pendulum rights itself. Every balancing robot, from a two wheeler to a humanoid on one foot, is doing exactly this.

lessons.title: The Angle Loop
lessons.goal: Stabilise the pendulum with a PD controller on angle and find the gain floor.
lessons.theory:
For the inverted pendulum there is a minimum `Kp`, not just a maximum. The controller has to produce more restoring acceleration than gravity is producing destabilising acceleration, so `Kp` must exceed roughly `g`, in the units of the linearised model.

Below that floor the robot falls no matter how well you tune everything else. Above it the loop is stabilisable, and `Kd` decides whether it settles or oscillates around vertical.

Measure how long it stays up, not where it ended, and give it a full minute. The final angle cannot carry this lesson: a spire that fell reports the 1.2 rad escape test rather than anything you controlled, and every gain above the floor reports zero, so two thirds of the table would be the same number twice. Time upright says both things, and it says how close to the floor you are, because it stretches as you approach: 4.6 s at `kp` 6, 16.4 s at 9, 34.5 s at 9.5, and the whole run from 9.82 upward. Four seconds is far too short to ask. At `kp` 9 the spire is still near vertical at 0.09 rad when the fourth second passes, and it is on the floor by the seventeenth.

`Kd` shows up in a different number. Above the floor with no rate term at all the spire never falls and never settles either, crossing vertical 126 times in the minute. Add rate feedback and the crossings fall to 60, and then to none.

This is the first loop in the course where a wrong gain means the machine is on the floor, not merely slow. Simulate before you power up.

lessons.title: Two Sensors, One Angle
lessons.goal: Fuse accelerometer and gyroscope with a complementary filter.
lessons.theory:
An MPU-6050 gives you two ways to know the tilt and both are wrong. The accelerometer measures gravity plus every bump the robot makes, so it is correct on average and unusable instantly. The gyroscope measures rotation rate cleanly but drifts when integrated, so it is correct instantly and useless after a minute.

The **complementary filter** takes the high frequency content from the gyro and the low frequency from the accelerometer: `angle = a * (angle + gyro*dt) + (1-a) * accel_angle`, with `a` around 0.98 at 200 Hz.

It is two lines and it outperforms a badly tuned Kalman filter on a balancing robot. Understand it before you reach for anything heavier.

class ComplementaryFilter:
    def __init__(self, alpha=0.98, angle=0.0):

lessons.title: Finding True Vertical

The angle your IMU calls zero is not the angle at which the robot stands still. Mounting tilt, a heavier battery on one side, uneven wheels, all shift the true balance point by a degree or two.

Run the balance loop with the wrong zero and the robot holds that wrong angle, which means it accelerates continuously in one direction until it hits a wall. The angle loop is doing its job perfectly.

The fix is a very slow outer trim: observe the average wheel velocity over several seconds and shift the angle setpoint until it is zero. Slow is essential. Anything fast enough to react within the angle loop's bandwidth will destabilise it.

import time

class RobotState:
    def __init__(self):
        self.angle = 0.0
        self.rate = 0.0
        self.position = 0.0
        self.velocity = 0.0
        self.stopped = False

    def stop(self):
        self.stopped = True

def run_loop(state, controller, duration=0.1, period=0.005):
    ticks = 0
    start = time.perf_counter()
    next_tick = start
    last = start
    try:
        while time.perf_counter() - start < duration:
            next_tick = next_tick + period
            delay = next_tick - time.perf_counter()
            if delay > 0.0:
                time.sleep(delay)
            now = time.perf_counter()
            dt = min(3.0 * period, max(0.5 * period, now - last))
            last = now
            controller(state, dt)
            ticks = ticks + 1
    finally:
        state.stop()
    return ticks

print(run_loop(RobotState(), lambda s, dt: None))
lessons.hint: The `finally` block must call `state.stop()` so an exception still kills the motors.

lessons.title: The Sense of Up
lessons.goal: Wire the complementary filter and gyro bias removal into the state estimator.
lessons.theory:
The estimator turns raw MPU-6050 samples into the two numbers the controller needs: tilt angle and tilt rate. Two steps, both easy to get wrong.

First, remove the gyro bias. Every MPU-6050 reports a nonzero rate while perfectly still, typically one or two degrees per second, and integrating that is what makes an uncalibrated robot drift off vertical in ten seconds. Average 500 samples at boot, with the robot held still, and subtract that constant forever after.

Feed it a robot that is actually turning, or the blend weight will not show at all. Hold the gyro at its bias and the filter's fixed point is the accelerometer angle for every `alpha` below 1, so 0.5, 0.9 and 0.98 all print the same line, and so does an `alpha` of zero, which is no filter at all. Give it a real 0.2 rad per second and the weights separate: the estimate settles at 0.081, 0.089 and 0.129, which is the accelerometer angle plus `alpha` times the rate step over one minus `alpha`. lessons.title: The Inner Loop
lessons.goal: Build the angle PID with derivative on measurement, output limits and back calculation.
lessons.theory:
The angle loop runs at 200 Hz, takes a tilt setpoint near zero, and produces a motor command. It is a PD loop with a small integral, because the residual mount offset is handled by the trim loop, not by this integral.

Use the gyro rate directly as the derivative rather than differentiating the filtered angle. It is a cleaner signal, it costs nothing, and it removes the derivative filter lag entirely. This is one of the few places where you have a real rate sensor and should use it.

Anti windup is mandatory here. This loop saturates every time the robot is nudged, and a windup on the balance axis means a fall.

class AngleLoop:
    def __init__(self, kp=40.0, ki=6.0, kd=2.2, tt=0.15, limit=1.0):
        self.kp = kp
        self.ki = ki
        self.kd = kd
        self.tt = tt
        self.limit = limit

lessons.title: The Kill Switch
lessons.goal: Add fall detection, tilt limits and a disarm path that resets every integrator.
lessons.theory:
A balancing robot that tips past about 35 degrees cannot recover. Continuing to drive the motors at that point achieves nothing except a fast slide into whatever is in front of it.

So the controller needs an armed state. Above the fall angle, disarm: zero the motors, reset every integrator, and stay disarmed until the robot is placed back near vertical and stable for a full second. Reset matters as much as the cut, because a disarmed loop keeps accumulating and rearms with a huge command otherwise.

lessons.title: When PID Is Not the Answer
lessons.goal: Recognise the four cases where a PID cannot work and name what replaces it.
lessons.theory:
PID is the right tool for a single input, single output, roughly linear plant with modest delay. Outside that box it is not merely hard to tune, it is the wrong shape.

**Long dead time.** When the delay is comparable to the time constant, as in a chemical bath or a long conveyor, any PID aggressive enough to be useful will oscillate. The answer is a Smith predictor or model predictive control, both of which carry an explicit model of the delay.

**Coupled axes.** A quadrotor cannot be controlled by four independent PIDs on four states that all interact, and neither can a chemical column where every valve moves every temperature. That is multivariable control, and the tools are state feedback like LQR or MPC.

**Hard constraints.** When the requirement is not a setpoint but a limit that must never be crossed, current, torque, a wall, PID has no way to express it. MPC optimises subject to constraints and that is exactly what it exists for.

**Strong nonlinearity.** A plant whose gain changes by a factor of ten across its range needs gain scheduling or feedback linearisation, not a single tune. And when the actuator is a relay, bang bang with hysteresis is better than a PID pretending it has a continuous output.
